items.title: Why a bare "RESULT: APPLIED" parses as nothing
items.body:
**Key: NEEDS_REVIEW, because the regex requires a dash followed by a reason.**

The RESULT regex is `/^result\s*:\s*([a-z_]+)\s*-\s*(.+)$/i`. Read it piece by piece: the word result, a colon, a status word, then a **dash** and at least one character of reason. `RESULT: APPLIED` has no dash, so the line does not match and is skipped. With nothing else to parse, the default NEEDS_REVIEW is returned. Exercise E1 asks you to prove this with a test.

Why the others are wrong:
- *APPLIED with submitted false*: the line never matches, so no APPLIED status is produced at all.
- *FAILED for an incomplete marker*: the parser has no "incomplete" rule; non-matching lines are just skipped.
- *APPLIED with "No reason provided"*: that fallback reason exists only in the **JSON** path, not in RESULT parsing.

This is also the difference from the Python sibling most likely to bite.

excerpts.quote: const match = line.match(/^result\s*:\s*([a-z_]+)\s*-\s*(.+)$/i); if (!match) { continue; }
**Check**: the status is `NEEDS_REVIEW`, not `APPLIED` — the regex requires `- <reason>`.

items.title: Which JSON candidate wins: fenced block or bare line
items.body:
**Key: the bare-line APPLIED object.**

`parseJsonOutcome` builds one list of candidates in two steps: first every fenced code block, then every bare line that starts with `{` and ends with `}`. Then it loops from the **end** of the list back to the start and returns the first one that validates. Bare lines were added last, so a valid bare line is checked before any fence. Here the bare APPLIED object wins.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The first candidate in the raw text*: position in the text does not matter; position in the list does, and the scan runs backwards.
- *Neither, ambiguous*: the parser has no ambiguity rule; it returns the first valid candidate it reaches.
- *The fenced FAILED block*: fences sit at the front of the list, so they are reached last.

The guide adds that this ordering "is currently enforced by nothing but the implementation"; exercise E2 asks you to write the test.

excerpts.quote: candidates.push(...lineObjects); for (let i = candidates.length - 1; i >= 0; i -= 1) {
fences are pushed first, bare lines after, scan is last-to-first). This ordering is currently enforced by nothing but the implementation.

items.title: What callJsonModel does when the JSON does not fit the schema
items.body:
**Key: it retries, telling the model its previous output was invalid for the schema.**

`callJsonModel` loops up to `parseRetries` extra times (default 2). Each try calls the provider, extracts JSON and runs `schema.parse(parsed)`. Zod throws if the keys do not match, the `catch` saves the error and replaces the prompt with one that says "Previous output was invalid JSON for this exact schema." Only a successful `schema.parse` returns; after the last failure the error is thrown.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Returns the object unvalidated*: the only `return` is `return schema.parse(parsed)`, so callers get a validated value or an error.
- *Strips unknown keys and fills defaults*: there is no repair step; a mismatch goes to `catch`.
- *Switches provider*: `provider` is read once from config before the loop and never changes.

excerpts.quote: return schema.parse(parsed); } catch (error) { lastError = error; userPrompt = `${messages.user}\n\nPrevious output was invalid JSON for this exact schema. Return only JSON and match schema keys exactly.`;
const { provider, model, temperature } = ctx.config.llm;

items.title: Why rewording the parse-failure message silently kills fallback
items.body:
**Key: auto-fallback for parse failures silently dies, and no test fails.**

`fallbackParseIndicator` in `index.ts` decides whether to hand a job to Codex by testing the *English text* of the reason: `/No RESULT line or valid JSON terminal output found/i`. That sentence is produced in `parsing.ts`. The two files agree only on a sentence; nothing shared ties them. Reword the message and the regex never matches again, so the parse-failure fallback stops happening. The guide's exercise E3 says no test fails: "that's the finding".

Why the others are wrong:
- *Fallback keys off NEEDS_REVIEW alone*: the function requires NEEDS_REVIEW **and** the regex match.
- *TypeScript fails to compile*: the indicator imports nothing about the message; it is a plain regex, which is why "the type system can't see the contract".
- *The parsing suite snapshots the reason*: E3's Check says no test fails.

The fix the guide asks for: one exported constant or a machine-readable marker used in both files, plus a test.

excerpts.quote: return outcome.status === 'NEEDS_REVIEW' && /No RESULT line or valid JSON terminal output found/i.test(outcome.reason);
**Check**: no test fails (that's the finding), yet auto-fallback is now dead code for the parse-failure case.

items.title: How rediscovering a URL updates the stored row
items.body:
**Key: salary keeps the stored value, while title is overwritten.**

Discovery inserts jobs with `onConflictDoUpdate` on `jobs.url`: if a row with that URL already exists, it is updated instead of duplicated. In the update, `excluded` means "the new values we tried to insert". Title is set to `excluded.title` with no condition. Salary uses `coalesce(excluded.salary, jobs.salary)`: SQL `coalesce` picks the first non-null value, so a missing new salary keeps the stored one.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Both overwritten, salary becomes null*: `coalesce` prevents the null from winning.
- *Both kept, never updated*: the conflict clause updates the row; title changes.
- *A second row is inserted*: the conflict target is the URL, so one URL means one row.

excerpts.quote: target: jobs.url, set: { title: sql`excluded.title`, salary: sql`coalesce(excluded.salary, ${jobs.salary})`,

items.title: What --dry-run actually guarantees
items.body:
**Key: nothing in code; the DRY_RUN rewrite only keeps the DB honest.**

In `index.ts`, after the agent has finished, an APPLIED outcome under `--dry-run` is rewritten to DRY_RUN with `submitted: false`. That happens *after* the browser work is done, so it cannot undo a real click. The only thing that stops a submission is the prompt asking the agent not to submit. The guide calls it "a prompt-level promise, not a code-level guarantee" and suggests the help text ("Run without final submission") should say so.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The parser refuses APPLIED in dry-run*: the parser does not know about dry-run; the rewrite is in `index.ts`, after parsing.
- *The MCP config omits the click tool*: the guide names the prompt as "the real protection"; no tool is removed.
- *Chrome opens read-only*: nothing in the guide or the code describes a read-only browser session.

excerpts.quote: options.dryRun && result.parsed.status === 'APPLIED' ? { ...result.parsed, status: 'DRY_RUN' as const, submitted: false, reason: 'Dry-run mode enforced' }
The real protection is the prompt telling the agent not to submit — the rewrite just keeps the DB honest if the agent ignores it.

items.title: What happens to an unknown status like EXPIRED
items.body:
**Key: the token is not one of the five statuses, so the output becomes NEEDS_REVIEW.**

`normalizeStatus` only accepts APPLIED, FAILED, CAPTCHA, NEEDS_REVIEW and DRY_RUN; anything else returns `null`. In `parseResultLine`, a `null` status means `continue`: the line is skipped. With no other valid marker in the output, `parseAgentOutcome` falls through to its default, NEEDS_REVIEW.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Stored as a new EXPIRED status*: EXPIRED is not in the `statuses` list, so it can never come out of the parser.
- *Throws a zod error that aborts the run*: zod only checks JSON shape; RESULT lines are matched by regex, and unknown tokens are skipped, not thrown.
- *Folded into FAILED like Python*: that is the Python sibling's behavior; the guide lists "No EXPIRED/LOGIN_ISSUE mapping" as a difference.

excerpts.quote: const statuses: ParsedOutcomeStatus[] = ['APPLIED', 'FAILED', 'CAPTCHA', 'NEEDS_REVIEW', 'DRY_RUN'];
Python folds those tokens into `FAILED` with a reason prefix; here `normalizeStatus()` only accepts the five canonical statuses and skips anything else.

items.title: When a FAILED job is picked up again for apply
items.body:
**Key: only when includeFailed is set.**

Read the query in `getJobsReadyToApply`. Three conditions always apply: the PDF exists (`isNotNull(jobs.pdfAt)`), the attempts are under the cap (`lt(jobs.applyAttempts, maxAttempts)`), and the status is one of an allowed set. That set is built with `or(...)`: no status yet, or NEEDS_REVIEW, and **FAILED only if `includeFailed` is true** (otherwise that slot is `undefined`, which drizzle leaves out). `includeFailed` defaults to `false`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Never: FAILED is terminal* and *No: never retried*: FAILED can be retried; the code includes it when the flag is on.
- *Yes, while under the attempts cap*: being under the cap is necessary but not enough; without the flag the status condition excludes FAILED.

excerpts.quote: includeFailed = false
or(isNull(jobs.applyStatus), includeFailed ? eq(jobs.applyStatus, 'FAILED') : undefined, eq(jobs.applyStatus, 'NEEDS_REVIEW')),

items.title: Why exit code 0 with garbage output does not fall back
items.body:
**Key: exit 0 means the agent believes it finished, so a rerun risks a duplicate application.**

The fallback condition is `claude.exitCode !== 0 && fallbackParseIndicator(claude.parsed)`. Both parts must be true. With exit 0, the first part is false, so the Claude result is kept (it will be NEEDS_REVIEW). This is on purpose: the agent may already have submitted the form, and sending the same job to Codex could apply twice. The guide calls this the subtlest line in the stage.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Exit 0 maps to APPLIED*: the status comes from the parser, which returns NEEDS_REVIEW when no marker is found; exit code is only used for the fallback decision.
- *Codex cannot attach to the Chrome session*: the guide gives the duplicate-application reason, not a Chrome limitation.
- *It does fall back*: the `&&` makes that false for exit 0.

excerpts.quote: if (claude.exitCode !== 0 && fallbackParseIndicator(claude.parsed)) {
a zero exit code with garbage output does **not** fall back. That is deliberate (exit 0 means the agent believes it finished; re-running risks a duplicate application)

items.title: Core idea: every stage keeps its own attempts, error and success mark
items.body:
Applybot never runs one giant job that either works or crashes. Each stage keeps three columns per job row: an attempts counter, an error message, and a success marker (a timestamp or file path). A stage picks a row when the success marker is still empty and the attempts counter is below the configured maximum.

Why this helps: one bad posting cannot stop the whole run. It fails, its counter goes up, its error is saved, and the next run tries again until the cap is reached. You can always look at the row and see what happened.

When you read `src/db/jobs.ts`, look for these three pieces in every "get jobs ready for stage X" query, and notice any extra conditions a stage adds on top of them (stage 6 has its own status column).

excerpts.quote: - attempts counter (e.g. `scoreAttempts`) - error field (e.g. `scoreError`) - success marker (e.g. `scoredAt`) Selection rule: success missing and attempts `< maxAttemptsPerStage`. This prevents one bad row from crashing the entire run.

readMore.why: The selection queries that implement this rule for each stage.

items.title: Why a parsed CAPTCHA after a non-zero exit does not go to Codex
items.body:
**Key: no: a parsed CAPTCHA is a terminal outcome.**

Under `--agent auto`, Codex runs in exactly two cases: `runClaude()` throws, or Claude exits non-zero **and** the parse is the specific "no marker found" NEEDS_REVIEW. Here Claude printed a valid `RESULT: CAPTCHA - blocked` line, so the parser returns CAPTCHA. `fallbackParseIndicator` checks for NEEDS_REVIEW, so it is false, and the `&&` fails. The Claude result is kept. The guide says CAPTCHA "never" triggers Codex, so one job never gets two submission attempts.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Any non-zero exit triggers fallback*: the exit code is only half of the condition.
- *CAPTCHA is retryable*: nothing in the fallback code treats CAPTCHA as retryable; the guide lists it with FAILED as terminal.
- *Only under --dry-run*: the fallback code does not look at `dryRun`; dry-run is applied after a result is chosen.

excerpts.quote: `FAILED`, `CAPTCHA`, and a genuine `NEEDS_REVIEW` never trigger Codex, so one job never gets two submission attempts.
const claude = await runClaude(); if (claude.exitCode !== 0 && fallbackParseIndicator(claude.parsed)) { result = await runCodex(); } else { result = claude; }

items.title: Why a JSON outcome beats a RESULT line
items.body:
**Key: APPLIED: the JSON path runs first and returns before RESULT lines are read.**

`parseAgentOutcome` has a fixed order. It calls `parseJsonOutcome` first. If any JSON candidate validates and has a known status, it returns right away. Only if JSON gives nothing does it call `parseResultLine`. Here the bare line `{"result":"APPLIED"}` is valid, so APPLIED is returned and the `RESULT: FAILED` line is never looked at. The guide notes "JSON precedence" is one of the three behaviors the parsing tests pin.

Why the others are wrong:
- *FAILED because RESULT is more explicit*: the code has no notion of "more explicit"; order decides.
- *NEEDS_REVIEW because markers cancel*: NEEDS_REVIEW is returned only when both paths find nothing.
- *FAILED because the last line wins*: "last line first" happens *inside* each path, but JSON is tried as a whole before any RESULT line.

excerpts.quote: const jsonOutcome = parseJsonOutcome(text); if (jsonOutcome) { return jsonOutcome; } const resultLine = parseResultLine(text);
three tests today covering case-insensitivity, JSON precedence and the NEEDS_REVIEW fallback.

items.title: Why a hallucinated APPLIED line is stored as submitted
items.body:
**Key: submitted true, because it defaults to status === APPLIED.**

In `parseResultLine`, the returned object sets `submitted: status === 'APPLIED'`. A RESULT line carries no separate submitted flag, so the parser simply assumes an APPLIED status means the form was submitted. The JSON path does the same when `submitted` is missing (`parsed.submitted ?? status === 'APPLIED'`). Nothing checks the claim, so the database marks the job applied "with no secondary evidence".

Why the others are wrong:
- *NEEDS_REVIEW because "ok" is short*: the regex only needs one character of reason (`(.+)`); "ok" matches.
- *submitted false because no flag*: the default is computed from the status, so it is true for APPLIED.
- *APPLIED pending a secondary check*: there is no secondary check; the guide notes the Python lineage stores `verification_confidence` and this schema does not.

excerpts.quote: status, reason: match[2].trim(), submitted: status === 'APPLIED'
a hallucinated `RESULT: APPLIED - ok` line marks the job applied in the DB with no secondary evidence.

items.title: Core idea: the agent must end with a machine-readable result
items.body:
In stage 6 an AI agent works in a real browser, then exits. Applybot cannot watch the form; it only reads the agent's text output. So there is a **contract**: the output must contain either a `RESULT:` line with a status and a reason, or a small JSON object with `result`, `reason` and `submitted`. The parser in `parsing.ts` turns that text into a status the database stores.

Read the parser top to bottom before the quizzes: it is short, and every status the database stores starts life as a line of agent text that this file accepted.

The ARCHITECTURE guide compares this parser with a Python sibling project. Reading the two side by side is a good way to see how a "contract" can drift.

excerpts.quote: Important contract: final agent output must include either: - `RESULT: <STATUS> - <reason>` - or JSON `{ "result": "...", "reason": "...", "submitted": true|false }`
Same six-stage design, same agent abstraction — but the parsers are **not** drop-in equivalents, and reading the two side by side is a good contracts exercise.

readMore.why: The whole parser is under 100 lines; read it top to bottom.

items.title: Start here: the seven-stage job pipeline and where to read
items.body:
Applybot is a command-line tool that finds job postings and works through them in stages: discover, enrich, score (an LLM rates the fit), tailor a resume, write a cover letter, render PDFs, and finally **apply**, where an AI agent (Claude or Codex) drives a browser to fill the form. Each stage reads and writes rows in one `jobs` table.

Suggested reading order:

1. **docs/intern/SYSTEM_ARCHITECTURE.md**: the runtime shape, the data flow and the retry model.
2. **docs/intern/src_db_jobs.md**: how rows are upserted and picked for each stage.
3. **docs/intern/src_shared_llm.md**: the one helper every LLM stage uses.
4. **docs/intern/src_stages_apply_index.md** and **docs/intern/src_stages_apply_agents_parsing.md**: stage 6, the riskiest part.
5. **docs/ARCHITECTURE.md**: the fallback rules, the differences from the Python sibling, the exercises E1-E3 and the reviewer's pushback list. Most quizzes come from here.

Keep the code open beside each guide; the guides name exact functions and you should read them.

excerpts.quote: This guide explains how the main modules fit together and where to read first.
